title: Optimal Monetary Policy When Agents Are Learning
abstract: We derive optimal monetary policy in a sticky price model when private agents follow adaptive learning. We show that this slight departure from rationality has important implications for policy design. The central bank faces a new intertemporal trade-off, not present under rational expectations: it is optimal to forego stabilizing the economy in the present in order to facilitate private sector learning and thus ease the future intratemporal inflation-output gap trade-offs. The policy recommendation is robust: the welfare loss entailed by optimal policy under learning if the private sector actually has rational expectations is much smaller than if the central bank mistakenly assumes rational expectations when in fact agents are learning.
summary_en: Standard optimal-monetary-policy models assume firms and households have rational expectations, but real agents learn over time. Molnár and Santoro show that when private agents are adaptive learners rather than fully rational, the central bank faces a new intertemporal trade-off: stabilising the economy aggressively today slows learning and worsens the inflation-output trade-off tomorrow. They derive a robust policy recommendation — accept some short-run instability to teach agents about the policy rule — and show the welfare cost of wrongly assuming rational expectations is much larger than the cost of wrongly assuming learning.
data_used: Sticky-price New Keynesian DSGE model with adaptive-learning agents; calibrated to standard quarterly US data (output gap, inflation, interest rate) for parameter values in the welfare comparisons.
policy_relevance: Direct implication for MNB and ECB monetary-policy frameworks: the central bank should weight teaching-the-private-sector-about-the-rule against immediate stabilisation, especially after regime changes (e.g., MNB's 2017 self-financing programme, ECB's 2021 strategy review). The asymmetric welfare loss — rational-expectations-policy-under-learning is much costlier than the reverse — argues for a precautionary bias toward learning-aware policy when expectations may be drifting.
